newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS - Mobil, Shell hope to cut costs with merger.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Mobil, Shell hope to cut costs with merger.

text.p: In a move they hope will cut costs, oil giants Mobil Corp. and Royal Dutch Shell Group's Shell Oil Co. agreed on Wednesday to merge their California exploration and production businesses by mid-1997.
The marriage would create the state's biggest producer.
"Our goal is to create a significant advantage in the California exploration and production business," said Mike Yeager, president of Mobil Exploration and Producing, U.S.
The two oil companies would own combined reserves of more than one billion barrels of oil equivalent and production of about 250,000 barrels per day (bpd) of oil equivalent.

The merger is the latest in a flurry of big oil reshuffling. Shell continues to negotiate with Texaco Inc about merging their U.S. downstream assets while Unocal Corp. last week said it would divest its California refineries.
In Europe, overproduction and falling profits have forced U.S. refiners such as Chevron Corp and Mobil to enter joint ventures with foreign energy companies this year.

"The upstream has been more profitable, but you have the downstream to live with too. You have to look throughout the whole company to see where you can cut costs," said Chevron's former chief economist, Bill Hermann.
Upstream operations refer to exploration and production of oil while downstream pertains to refining and marketing.
In California, much of the oil owned by Mobil and Shell's production unit, CalResources LLC, lies in adjacent fields.
That gives both companies a chance to ease the high costs of wringing oil from aging oil fields, experts said.
Sixty percent of Mobil's 100,000 bpd heavy crude production is next to Shell assets, while half of Shell's 150,000 bpd output lies beside Mobil.
"Certainly, being more efficient with what we have is the more important part" of the merger, Yeager said.
Mobil estimates the typical cost of squeezing more heavy oil from the fields runs into hundreds of millions of dollars.
That cost, which accounts for roughly $7 to $8 per barrel, can become difficult in a period of falling refinery margins and higher world crude prices.
"We've got a big, expensive business," Yeager concedes.
But analysts say prospects for native, or "heavy" crudes, have improved in recent years as more lucrative and "lighter" grades from Alaska have seen production decline.
"Rather than give up on California, I would say they have newer techniques...and they get more of the oil out of the ground," said Chevron's Hermann.
Twenty years ago, California producers expected to yield 10 percent from reserves, but now the figure is 60 percent.
Production of Alaska North Slope (ANS) crude has fallen from a peak of 2.0 million bpd in 1988 to 1.5 million this year.
"(ANS) will be less of a price threat," Yeager said.
And that will let California crudes stay closer to benchmark crudes such as West Texas Intermediate, which currently costs about $7 to $8 more per barrel.
"I think the California oil industry is on the verge of the next step in values," Yeager said.
